exhibits.title: The Hat and the Vee
exhibits.text:
Two brass mechanisms stand back to back on a single plinth, twins that undo each other. Between them floats a short rod strung with beads — a plain list of numbers, a coordinate vector, the humblest way to write a direction of motion.

The first mechanism is the HAT. It reaches out, takes the rod of numbers, and LIFTS it — and as it rises the beads unfold and arrange themselves into a square frame of gears, a MATRIX, spinning gently in place. The numbers have not changed their meaning; they have only put on a richer costume. Watch the frame it builds: it is always SKEW — cross it against its own reflection and the two cancel exactly, each gear opposite its own negative across the diagonal. This is the shape of pure turning, and only such frames will do for the turns of this world.

The second mechanism is the VEE. It takes the spinning matrix-frame and READS it back DOWN — plucking out the handful of numbers that define it, letting them fall back onto the rod as plain beads. The costume comes off; the list returns.

Round they pass the rod between them, hat lifting numbers into a matrix, vee reading the matrix back into numbers, neither ever losing a thing. The same element of motion, dressed two ways: as a list you can store and add, and as a matrix the deeper machinery of the palace knows how to set in motion.

exhibits.title: The Hat Operator
exhibits.text:
An element of the tangent space — the flat space of allowed motions — can be written as a plain list of numbers, a coordinate vector in ℝⁿ. Convenient for storing and adding, but it is not the form the deeper machinery wants. The HAT operator, written with a small caret (v ↦ v̂, read 'v-hat'), lifts that coordinate vector UP into its MATRIX form: same information, richer costume.

For the elements that describe TURNING, the matrix hat builds is always SKEW-SYMMETRIC — it equals the negative of its own transpose, Aᵀ = −A. Such a matrix has zeros down its diagonal and mirror entries that are exact negatives across it. That single property is the algebraic fingerprint of a pure rotation-in-waiting.

The worked 2D example, small enough to hold in the hand. A single number a — one coordinate, the amount of turn — is lifted by the hat into the 2×2 matrix

    a  ↦  [ 0  −a ]
           [ a   0 ]

Check it: the diagonal is zero, and the off-diagonal pair is a and −a, negatives of each other — skew-symmetric, exactly as required. One number has become a 2×2 frame, and that frame is precisely the object the next mechanism upstairs, the exponential map, knows how to turn into an actual rotation of the plane.

exhibits.title: The Vee Operator
exhibits.text:
The VEE operator, written with a small wedge (A ↦ Aˇ, read 'A-vee'), runs the hat backwards. Hand it the MATRIX form — a skew-symmetric frame — and it reads it back DOWN into the plain coordinate vector that defines it, plucking out the handful of free numbers and discarding the scaffolding of zeros and forced negatives. Matrix in, list of numbers out.

It is the exact inverse of the hat: apply hat then vee, or vee then hat, and you return to precisely where you began. (v̂)ˇ = v, always.

The 2D example, run in reverse. Take the skew matrix

    [ 0  −a ]
    [ a   0 ]      ↦   a

The vee ignores the mandatory zeros on the diagonal, notes that the two off-diagonal entries are just a and its negative, and reports the single free number a. The costume is removed; the coordinate is recovered.

Why keep both directions? Because the two forms serve two masters. The matrix form is what the exponential map eats to reach the curved surface. The vector form is what ordinary arithmetic and plain storage prefer — you cannot easily add or average matrices constrained to be skew, but you can add and average their lists of numbers with abandon. Vee lets an element of the algebra be handled, stored, and reckoned with as an ordinary vector, then handed back to hat when the machinery needs it.

exhibits.title: The Three Spaces
exhibits.text:
Step back and count the worlds this wing shuttles between. There are THREE, and four operators ferry motion among them.

  1. PLAIN COORDINATES — ℝⁿ, a list of numbers. Where arithmetic lives: add, average, scale, take a small straight step. Simple and unconstrained.
  2. The MATRIX ALGEBRA — the same element wearing its skew-symmetric matrix costume. The form the exponential map can act upon.
  3. The CURVED SURFACE — the space of valid configurations, where every point is an honest state of the world.

The ferries:

    ℝⁿ  ──hat (∧)──▶  matrix algebra  ──exp──▶  curved surface
    ℝⁿ  ◀──vee (∨)──  matrix algebra  ◀──log──  curved surface

Hat and vee cross the first bridge (coordinates ↔ matrix); exp and log cross the second (matrix ↔ surface). And the grand strategy of the whole wing falls out of the picture: keep your configurations VALID by living on the curved surface, but do ALL your arithmetic down in flat ℝⁿ where numbers behave. To take a step, run the full relay — log and vee down to a plain vector, reckon there, then hat and exp back up to a valid point on the surface. Three spaces, four ferries, one round trip.

exhibits.caption: Three spaces, connected by two bridges. Hat (∧) and vee (∨) ferry between the plain coordinate vector in ℝⁿ and its skew-symmetric matrix form; exp and log ferry between that matrix form and a point on the curved surface. Store and do arithmetic in flat ℝⁿ; hat then exp to reach a valid surface point, log then vee to come back.

exhibits.title: Lift and Lower, the Antisymmetry Made Plain
exhibits.caption: The two mechanisms drawn as pictures. Panel (a) is the smallest case: a single number a — one coordinate, the amount of turn — lifted by the hat into the 2×2 frame with zero on the diagonal and the mirror pair a and −a across it. Read the colours and the skewness is plain to the eye: the greyed zeros run down the diagonal, and every off-diagonal entry faces its own negative. Panel (b) is the 3D case, the vector (x, y, z) raised into the 3×3 frame — zeros down the diagonal again, and each entry above the diagonal answered by its negative below, so that Aᵀ = −A exactly. That single property, zero diagonal and negated mirror, is the whole fingerprint of a pure turn. The vee runs every arrow backwards, plucking the free numbers back out of the frame and discarding the forced zeros. Panel (c) sets the wing in one figure: three spaces at the corners of a triangle, four ferries along its edges. Hat and vee cross the near bridge — plain coordinates to matrix and back; exp and log cross the far one — matrix to the curved surface and back. Store and reckon in flat Rⁿ where numbers behave; hat then exp to climb to a valid point, log then vee to return.
